Text: I would recommend Georges Perec's Life: A User's Manual. It's a lengthy and delightful and bewildering book that chronicles what happens in a single apartment building in Paris on a single day in the 1970s, though there are lots of digressions into the past, and the future, and to other locales. Perec was a member of the OULIPO group, who were a bunch of interesting, often mathematically-minded authors who were determined to discover the fullest possible scope of "literature under constraint." Some would write stuff using only certain letters; some would take the same basic plot and rewrite it in a hundred different forms; some (like Perec, in this case) would develop enormous lists of objects, people, and places - and then set them against a rigorous chart based on a "knight's tour" (like in Chess) of a hundred-square board - with the firm intention of including all of them in the final work, in a highly specific but also random order. Unlike certain others who would do such things out of spite for the general reader, Perec and his compatriots took as one of their first principles the idea that whatever literature resulted from their plans had to be entertaining. Anyway, it is a long, beautiful, hilarious, sad, unusual book, in which any number of weird and awesome things happen. I recommend it unreservedly to anyone in the entire world. You will not regret it.

Text: The very first sentence from Gideon the Ninth.In the myriadic year of our Lord- the ten thousandth year of the King Undying, the kindly Prince of Death!- Gideon Nav packed her sword, her shoes, and her dirty magazines, and she escaped from the House of the Ninth. Utter perfection. We're also reassured that these books absolutely will not be boring. The next few pages are similarly packed with all sorts of worldbuilding, character development, and so on and so forth. In fact Tamsyn Muir's protagonists never pause to dump exposition at the reader- why would they, you and I would never stop in our kitchen to ruminate on the inner workings and history of the refrigerator. Every crucial detail has to be wrestled out of offhanded comments and vague references to events or sciences the reader is not privy to, so Muir can play with what the reader does and does not know at all times. Text: You can argue where the line is blurred between reinterpretation and misinterpretation, but it's happened to a lot of dystopian fiction. 1984 was written as a pretty direct "It Can't Happen Here" style critique of the Soviet Union, and is now seen as a general warning on surveillance. Text:
The Smiling, Proud Wanderer by Jin Yong.
Back when it was written (1967 - 1969) it was considered by many as a political allegory disguised as a fantasy Wuxia novel. There were a couple of differing interpretations, some of which saw the characters as parallels to political players in mainland China, which was seeing absolute carnage. Other interpretations likened characters to international players, seeing parallels between novel characters and the US, UK, USSR and China.
Many of those parallels are now lost on modern readers. However, the book has remained ageless despite the immediate political allegories no longer being relevant. Jin Yong himself believed that politics is everchanging but human nature is intransigent, therefore books should talk about human nature and not the specifics of politics to stay relevant.
In this sense, The Smiling, Proud Wanderer is successful. While the political allegories are no longer pointed, its discussion of themes is still relevant today: destructiveness of political ambition, deceptiveness of public image, impacts of cults of personality, corruptive nature of power, role of an escapist pursuit of freedom in an environment of political deterioration etc.

Text:
I, Claudius' by Robert Graves changed the interpretation of Classic Roman history.
Before that, the commonly accepted view by most historians was of emperor Claudius as an idiot-king, as described by Edward Gibbon, who referenced Seneca as a primary source, even though Seneca was biased against Claudius. When the Graves book came out, there was quite a bit of fuss and controversy among the Classics historians about him re-writing history. After the fuss died down, the new view was grudgingly acknowledged.
